decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of referencing as a deliberate practice is assumed. The learner is early in their studies and has met 'reference your sources' as an instruction without a clear sense of what it asks or why it matters; teach from first principles.

subThemes.label: What referencing is: acknowledging where the knowledge in your work comes from
Why references matter: evidence of your research and a part of academic integrity, not just avoiding plagiarism

What a reference is made of: author, date, title and the conventions that format it
Referencing when you quote and when you paraphrase: in-text references in both cases
Setting references out accurately and consistently, and the errors that creep in from copy-paste

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what referencing is and why it matters: the purpose behind the practice. Second, referencing styles and the parts of a reference: the main styles and what every reference is built from. Third, referencing accurately: how to acknowledge a source when you quote and when you paraphrase. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about referencing at university: what it is, why it matters, and how to do it accurately. By the end you will be able to explain what referencing is and why it matters, recognise the main referencing styles and what a reference is made of, and reference your sources accurately when you quote and when you paraphrase.

Referencing is not a box-ticking chore added at the end of an essay. 'Reference your sources' is one of the first instructions you meet at university, and getting it right credits the people whose ideas you use, shows a tutor the reading behind your work, and keeps you on the right side of academic integrity.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain what referencing is and why it matters, recognise the main styles and the parts of a reference, reference accurately when quoting and paraphrasing.

practiceConnection.academic: Referencing is a habit academic work is built on. Every essay that draws on reading, every report that cites evidence, every piece of work where you use someone else's idea, relies on acknowledging where that idea came from. Build the habit now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the professional work that later expects you to credit your sources.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced courses on this pathway take you from referencing into citation practice and into academic integrity in its own right. Going wider: the same habits underpin Academic Writing, Criticality and Researching, where you put referencing to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Referencing is no longer a vague chore: it is a practice you understand and can carry out. You can explain what referencing is - acknowledging where the knowledge in your work comes from - and why it matters, from crediting authors and academic integrity to showing a tutor the scope of your reading. You can recognise the main referencing styles and the parts every reference is built from. And you can reference accurately when you quote and when you paraphrase. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, referencing is something you practise in every module. Each time you draw on a reading, quote a source or paraphrase an idea, the habit is at work. It is also what academic and professional life rewards: crediting your sources and evidencing your claims accurately builds the trust that serious work depends on, well beyond your degree.
